title: Area II review: Preflight Procedures
intro: These questions mix all five Tasks of Area II, from the preflight walk-around to the before-takeoff check. Many of them join two Tasks in one real situation on the ramp, the taxiway or the run-up pad.

questions.q: Halfway through your taxi, Ground changes your route to taxiways you have never used, with a runway crossing. Your passenger keeps chatting. What is the best way to handle it?
options: Keep rolling and work it out as you go, so you don't hold up other traffic
Answer "Roger" and follow the taxiway signs until you see the runway
Stop if needed, write down the new route, read it back, and trace it on the airport diagram before you go on
Follow your usual route, since you know it well and it ends at the same runway
questions.why: Any change to the taxi route must be fully understood, and cockpit occupants should be reminded to keep a sterile cockpit [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(b), (d)]]. Read back with your call sign and runway, not just "Roger" [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(4)]]. If anything conflicts or you are in doubt, don't continue the taxi [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

questions.q: Your flight school's airplane is used for paid lessons. Its last inspection was an annual done at 3,210.0 hours time in service, 8 months ago. It now shows 3,312.0 hours. May your instructor give you a paid lesson in it today?
options: Yes. The annual is good for 12 calendar months, and that covers lessons too.
No. It has flown 102 hours since its last inspection, so it needs a 100-hour or annual inspection first.
Yes. The rule allows 10 extra hours, so it is legal until 3,320.0 hours.
Yes, as long as you and the instructor find nothing wrong on the preflight.
questions.why: An airplane used for flight instruction for hire, in an airplane the instructor or school provides, needs an annual or 100-hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours of time in service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. The 10-hour allowance is only for flying to a place where the inspection can be done [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

questions.q: On a warm, humid day you check carburetor heat during the run-up in a trainer with a fixed-pitch propeller. The rpm drops, then slowly climbs back up over the next several seconds. What does this tell you?
options: Carburetor ice was present, and the heat is melting it
The carburetor heat valve is stuck closed
One magneto is not firing correctly
No carburetor ice was present; this is the normal result
questions.why: With a fixed-pitch prop, if ice is present the rpm drops and then gradually rises as the ice melts. With no ice, the rpm drops and then stays steady [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

questions.q: A passenger brings her 5-year-old son and the booster seat he uses in the car. It has no FAA approval label. May he ride in the booster seat?
options: Yes. Any child seat is fine if it is tied to an airplane seat with the seat belt.
Yes, but only if it is installed in a front seat.
Yes, as long as he sits in it on his mother's lap.
No. Booster-type seats are not approved for use in aircraft unless they are FAA-approved.
questions.why: Booster-type child restraints, vest- and harness-type restraints and lap-held restraints are not approved for aircraft, unless the device itself has FAA approval [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)(B)(4)]]. Only a child who has not reached the second birthday may be held on an adult's lap [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]].

questions.q: It is 30 minutes after sunset. You are ready to start the engine. Per the AFH, which lights should be on before you engage the starter?
options: Taxi light and strobes, but no position lights until takeoff
Only the landing light, so people ahead can see you
Anti-collision (beacon) lights and position lights
No lights, so the battery has full power for cranking
questions.why: Anti-collision lights should be on before every engine start, and for night operations the position lights too [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. From sunset to sunrise you may not operate an aircraft without lighted position lights [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]].

questions.q: Ground clears you to Runway 22, and ATIS gives the wind as 240 at 12 knots. Your first taxiway runs west, so you roll along on a heading of 270. How should you hold the controls in your nosewheel airplane?
options: Yoke turned right, elevator neutral
Yoke turned left, elevator neutral
Yoke turned right and pushed forward
Yoke turned left and pushed forward
questions.why: A wind from 240 while heading 270 comes from 30 degrees to your left, a quartering headwind from the left. Hold the upwind (left) aileron up by turning the yoke left [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. In a nosewheel airplane the elevator stays neutral in a headwind [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].

questions.q: Your airplane's engine burns 100LL. Your fuel sample looks clear, smells like kerosene, and feels oily on your fingers. What is the most likely problem?
options: It is probably jet fuel. Don't fly: the engine may run long enough to take off and then fail.
It is water. Keep sampling until the sample turns blue.
It is 80/87, which is an approved substitute for 100LL.
It is 100LL. The blue dye is just hard to see, so the fuel is fine.
questions.why: Jet fuel is clear or straw-colored, has a distinctive non-gasoline odor and is oily to the touch. A piston engine on jet fuel may start and power the airplane until it is airborne, then fail after takeoff [[24:44|AFH 2-7]].

questions.q: Tower offers you a quick departure with a 6-knot tailwind. Your POH gives a 1,200-foot ground roll with no wind, and you lift off at 60 knots. Using the PHAK rule of thumb, about how long will the ground roll be?
options: About 1,000 feet
About 1,260 feet
About 1,450 feet
About 1,320 feet
questions.why: A 6-knot tailwind is 10 percent of the 60-knot takeoff speed. A tailwind that is 10 percent of takeoff airspeed adds about 21 percent to the takeoff distance [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]. 1,200 x 1.21 = 1,452 feet.

questions.q: You plan a 3.5-hour cross-country flight with two friends. Per the PHAK, how often should you run the 5 P check (Plan, Plane, Pilot, Passengers, Programming) in cruise?
options: Only before takeoff and again before landing
Every 15 minutes, along with each fuel tank switch
About every hour, because the flight is longer than 2 hours
Once, at the halfway point of the trip
questions.why: The PHAK says that if the flight is longer than 2 hours, the 5 P check should be done hourly [[1:53|PHAK 2-14]].

questions.q: On a cold morning, the engine fires and you quickly push the throttle well forward to keep it running. It backfires. What is the main cause?
options: Holding the brakes too firmly during the start
Too little primer before the start
The starter staying engaged after the start
Opening the throttle too much after the engine fired
questions.why: Too much throttle after the engine has fired is the main cause of backfiring during starting. Open the throttle gradually while the engine is cold [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

questions.q: At 1600 you find that the left position light is out. You plan to leave now and fly back home after sunset. There is no MEL. Which is true?
options: It is fine. You leave in daylight, so you can defer the light for the whole trip.
You can't make the trip as planned. Position lights are required from sunset to sunrise, so the return leg after dark is not legal.
It is fine. Only the right position light is required at night.
It is fine at night as long as the anti-collision light works.
questions.why: Approved position lights are required for VFR flight at night [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(2)]], and you may not operate from sunset to sunrise without lighted position lights [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]]. An item required by 91.205 for the kind of flight can't be deferred [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

questions.q: Your radio fails while you taxi at a towered airport in daylight. The tower aims a flashing white light at you. What does it mean, and how do you acknowledge it?
options: Cleared to taxi; acknowledge by flashing your landing light
Exercise extreme caution; acknowledge by rocking your wings
Return to your starting point on the airport; acknowledge by flashing your landing light
Return to your starting point on the airport; acknowledge by moving the ailerons or rudder
questions.why: For an aircraft on the ground, flashing white means return to starting point on airport [[1:359|PHAK 14-25]]. In daylight, acknowledge light signals by moving the ailerons or rudder; flashing your lights is the night method [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13e]].

questions.q: On a long cruise leg, you loosen your shoulder harness to reach a chart in the back seat. Your seat belt stays fastened. Is that allowed?
options: Yes. En route you must keep your seat belt fastened; the shoulder harness is required during takeoff and landing.
No. Both the seat belt and the shoulder harness must stay fastened the whole flight.
No. The shoulder harness must stay on en route, but the seat belt may come off.
Yes, and in smooth air you may also unfasten the seat belt.
questions.why: Required flight crewmembers must keep the safety belt fastened at their station during takeoff, landing and en route, and keep the shoulder harness fastened during takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.105]].

questions.q: You pull into the run-up area. A regional jet is holding short of the runway, and the only open spot is about 150 feet behind it and off to one side. What should you do?
options: Take the spot. At 150 feet you are well clear of jet blast.
Take the spot, but point your tail at the jet so your prop blast goes toward it.
Take the spot, since jet blast only matters while the jet is taking off.
Wait or pick a spot well away from the jet; a small airplane there once got a wing and prop strike when the jet powered up.
questions.why: Give yourself ample distance behind a jet. In one case, a small aircraft doing a run-up 150 feet behind and to the side of an airliner holding short had a wing and prop strike when the airliner powered up [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.3.4]]. A run-up spot should be clear of other aircraft [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

questions.q: After a cold-weather start, you forget to lock the primer knob. What can happen in flight?
options: It can make the fuel-air mixture too lean
It can vibrate out of position and make the fuel-air mixture too rich
It can turn off one magneto
It can keep the starter engaged
questions.why: Lock the primer when it is not in use. If the knob is free to move, it may vibrate out of position in flight and cause an excessively rich fuel-air mixture [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]].

questions.q: Your club's airplane has a recurring airworthiness directive (AD) inspection, and the logbook shows it is overdue. The club manager says it can wait until next week. Can you fly it today?
options: Yes. The owner is responsible for ADs, so the renter pilot is not affected.
Yes. ADs are only advice from the manufacturer.
No. Anyone who operates an aircraft that doesn't meet an applicable AD is in violation, each time it is flown.
Yes, if you stay in the traffic pattern and carry no passengers.
questions.why: The owner or operator is primarily responsible for AD compliance [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]], but anyone who operates a product that doesn't meet an applicable AD violates the rule each time it is operated [[60:125|14 CFR 39.7, 39.9]].

questions.q: After landing at night, you turn off the runway and follow taxiway centerline lights that alternate green and yellow. What do they tell you?
options: You are clear of the runway and may stop for your after-landing checklist
You are still in the runway environment or ILS critical area
The taxiway ahead is closed
You are on a low-visibility taxi route
questions.why: Lead-off lights alternate green and yellow from the runway centerline to one light past the runway holding position or ILS critical area holding position. They warn you that you are still within the runway environment or ILS critical area [[1:352|PHAK 14-18]].

questions.q: You are about to press the NAV button so the autopilot follows your GPS course. Per the RMH, what should you do first?
options: Press it, then watch to see what the airplane does
Know what the airplane should do once you press it
Disconnect the autopilot, then press NAV
Switch the GPS to a VOR source
questions.why: The RMH steps are Anticipate, Act, Verify. First understand the system well enough to know what should happen before you push a button or turn a knob [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

questions.q: During the run-up you check the flight controls. Your passenger's camera bag on her lap stops the yoke from coming all the way back. What should you do?
options: Stow and secure the bag, then check full control travel again
Go ahead, and ask her to move the bag if you need more back yoke in flight.
Check full travel with the rudder only and continue.
Nothing. You rarely need full back yoke, so partial travel is fine.
questions.why: Flight controls must be checked through their entire range in all directions; less than full movement is not acceptable [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]. Baggage loading and security should be supervised by the pilot [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

questions.q: The engine is slow to start on a cold morning. After a long cranking attempt you smell burning insulation. What does this most likely mean?
options: The engine is flooded; keep cranking with the throttle open
It is the normal smell of cold oil warming up
The starter has been cranked too long; stop and let it cool
The alternator is charging the battery
questions.why: Starters are not built for continuous duty. The smell of burning insulation may mean the cranking time was exceeded. Avoid cranking longer than 30 seconds without a cool-down of at least 30 seconds to 1 minute [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

questions.q: You leave your paper charts at home and use only a tablet EFB for a VFR flight. Under AC 91-78A, which is true?
options: The FAA must approve the tablet before you can use it under Part 91
Outdated charts on the tablet are fine for VFR as long as GPS works
The app company, not the pilot, is responsible for keeping the charts current
You, the pilot, must verify that the navigation and performance information is current and valid
questions.why: An EFB may replace paper when the information used for navigation or performance planning is current, up to date and valid, as verified by the pilot. No formal operational approval is needed if the AC's guidelines are followed [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1, 9.2]].

questions.q: You land for fuel on a trip. Your two passengers are still in their seats when the fuel truck pulls up. What does the AFH advise?
options: Have the passengers get out, and watch the fueling yourself to check the fuel, the amount and the caps
Keep the passengers buckled in so they stay off the busy ramp
Let line service handle it and check the fuel gauges before takeoff
Stay in the cockpit with the passengers so they don't wander
questions.why: It is advisable to remove all passengers from the aircraft and witness the refueling to make sure the correct fuel and quantity go in and the caps and cowls are secured [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

questions.q: Ground clears you to cross Runway 10. As you near the hold line, a line of red in-pavement lights along the taxiway centerline, running from the hold line toward the runway, comes on. What should you do?
options: Keep going, since your ATC clearance overrides the lights
Keep going, but cross the runway quickly
Stop, then continue on your own once the lights go off
Stop, tell ATC the lights are on, and confirm your clearance
questions.why: Runway status lights are red and show it is unsafe to enter or cross a runway; they never give a clearance [[1:353|PHAK 14-19]]. Never cross illuminated red lights: notify ATC and re-confirm the clearance, and don't proceed when they go off without an ATC clearance [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6d]].

questions.q: A large airplane just did a touch-and-go on your runway in a light quartering wind. Per the AIM, how long should you wait before your takeoff?
options: At least 2 minutes
No wait. Wake turbulence comes only from airplanes that take off.
About 30 seconds
Only until the large airplane has turned crosswind
questions.why: After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go, vortices can settle and drift along the runway, especially in light quartering winds. Allow at least 2 minutes before your takeoff or landing [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b8]].
